strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: exposure bias and compounding errors in autoregressive diffusion-based robot world models, which limits their use as simulators for policy evaluation and improvement.

Provides a concrete adaptation of a recent contrastive RL objective (DiffusionNFT) to the x0-prediction EDM/robot-world-model setting, with a derivation and an attempt to preserve theoretical guarantees.

Introduces a sensible training protocol for autoregressive video world models: variable-length shared prefixes and K branched candidate continuations, allowing reward-based comparison from a common evolving context.
Designs a multi-view perceptual reward (LPIPS, SSIM, PSNR) and includes masked object-centric and robot-centric evaluations, which help show gains are not merely background preservation.
Empirical results on DROID are strong and consistent: improvements over WPE, IRASim, and Ctrl-World across metrics, ~98% paired comparison wins, and an 80% preference rate in a blind human study.

The paper is generally well organized, includes ablations and an appendix with derivation and implementation details, and discusses limitations (computational overhead, lack of physical/geometric constraints).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core RL objective is taken from DiffusionNFT, and the main new elements are adaptations (x0 parameterization, autoregressive prefix branching, multi-view perceptual rewards) rather than a fundamentally new algorithm. The contemporary work [36] already applies contrastive RL post-training to a world model with prefix rollouts.

The theoretical claim that convergence guarantees carry over exactly is overstated. Theorem 1 characterizes the minimizer of the proposed loss under ideal assumptions (unlimited data/capacity, reward as an optimality probability), but does not prove iterative convergence or expected-reward improvement. In practice the reward is a normalized perceptual score, not P(o=1|x0,c), so the theoretical interpretation is not directly applicable.

The reward design is not convincingly justified. In the ablation, the combined reward never decisively outperforms single-metric rewards; LPIPS-only, SSIM-only, and PSNR-only variants each win on their own axes and sometimes overall. The weighting of metrics and views appears largely heuristic.

The ablation table for group size/best-of-N contradicts the final model choice: 'No best of N' and 'Best of 2' outperform the used 'Best of 5 (Ours)' across all reported metrics, yet the main model still uses Best-of-5. The justification of efficiency and stable signals is not supported by evidence, and the final results may be unnecessarily suboptimal.

Evaluation is limited to the DROID dataset and the Ctrl-World backbone. WPE and IRASim numbers are largely inherited from prior work rather than retrained under identical conditions, and there is no cross-dataset, cross-backbone, or cross-embodiment validation. Masked evaluations may also rely on ground-truth segmentation, which can overstate object-position fidelity.

The main paper does not demonstrate the claimed benefit for downstream policy evaluation or policy improvement; that analysis is relegated to the appendix. This weakens the central motivation that persistent world models enable better robot simulation and policy development.

The human preference study is useful but limited: only 8 expert users, only a two-way comparison against the baseline, and participants could choose which videos to rate. The 95% CI [72%,100%] and moderate inter-rater kappa suggest the study is supportive but not as strong as the headline 80% preference rate implies.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: exposure bias and closed-loop degradation in action-conditioned autoregressive video world models for robotics.
The motivation is clear and well illustrated: the paper explains the train/test mismatch and shows qualitative failures where objects and robot arms decohere over long rollouts.
The proposed RL post-training pipeline is sensible: shared prefix rollout, independent candidate branching, group-normalized rewards, and LoRA/action-encoder updates.
Adapting contrastive denoising post-training to x0-prediction EDM-style world models is a practically relevant extension, even if the theoretical novelty is limited.
The multi-view perceptual reward combining LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR with group normalization is a reasonable engineering design for dense rollout reward.
The empirical study is broad in some respects: DROID evaluation across external/wrist cameras, object/robot-masked metrics, and a human preference study.
The human 2AFC/ELO study provides useful complementary evidence, reporting an 80% preference rate and a strong paired-comparison p-value.
The appendix includes a derivation, ablations, pseudocode, and a small policy-evaluation correlation study, showing some effort toward transparency and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core method is incremental relative to prior work: it adapts DiffusionNFT [42] to an x0-prediction world model and adds autoregressive branching/rewards. Contemporary WorldCompass [36] already applies contrastive RL post-training with a prefix-rollout strategy to a world model, and this paper does not compare against it despite sharing the core paradigm.

The theoretical claims are substantially overstated. The main text claims that convergence guarantees carry over exactly and implies policy-improvement guarantees, but Theorem 1 only characterizes the population minimizer of a contrastive loss under unrealistic assumptions such as unlimited data/capacity and a reference model equal to the posterior mean. It does not prove convergence of online RL training, finite-sample behavior, or practical policy improvement.

The data split is ambiguous and may be invalid. Rewards during post-training are computed against 'held-out ground-truth frames,' while evaluation uses Ctrl-World's held-out validation split. It is unclear whether the same validation ground truth is used for both reward computation and evaluation; if so, the reported results are contaminated. The paper must specify the train/val/test splits and the source of reward ground truth.

Baseline comparison is inconsistent and potentially misleading. Table 1 compares against a reproduced Ctrl-World with PSNR 23.02 rather than the reported Ctrl-World* PSNR 23.56, while the reproduced LPIPS 0.081 is better than the reported 0.091. The claimed 1.40 dB and 14% LPIPS gains shrink or change when using the strongest reported baseline, and the reproduction discrepancy is not explained.

The closest competing method, WorldCompass [36], is absent from all quantitative comparisons. Since the paper itself acknowledges that [36] shares the core motivation and training paradigm, the state-of-the-art claim is not well supported without a direct comparison.

Ablations undermine the chosen default configuration. Table 6 shows that 'No best of N' and 'Best of 2' outperform the selected 'Best of 5 (Ours)' on most metrics, yet the main method uses the weaker setting. Table 11 similarly suggests policy EMA helps but is not used. These choices need stronger justification or correction.

Most tables lack error bars or statistical variability. Many reported differences are tiny, e.g., combined reward versus SSIM-only reward in Table 4, or KL regularization in Table 9, so it is impossible to judge whether the improvements are significant.
The wrist-camera results are incomplete: WPE and IRASim are not evaluated on the wrist camera, so the claim that the method outperforms all baselines on all metrics is not established across views.

The object- and robot-centric evaluation lacks detail. It is unclear how RoboEngine masks are obtained, whether masks come from ground truth or generated frames, and how they are aligned across views. This matters because masked metrics are used to argue that gains are task-relevant rather than background-driven.

The human preference study is small and limited: only 8 in-house expert users, only against the Ctrl-World baseline, and moderate inter-rater agreement (κ≈0.4). It supports the main quantitative result only weakly by itself.

Evaluation is limited to one dataset (DROID) and one base model (Ctrl-World). There is no cross-dataset or cross-backbone generalization, and the downstream policy-evaluation evidence is relegated to a small appendix study rather than the main claims.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code release or detailed reward/split information is provided, and the method requires 8 H200 GPUs for 3 days for what appear to be modest gains over the reproduced baseline.
There are minor clarity issues in the notation and algorithm, e.g., Algorithm 1 mixes x0, xσ, and overwritten candidate notation, making the exact update harder to verify than necessary.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: exposure bias and compounding errors in autoregressive, action-conditioned robot world models.
Introduces a principled RL post-training scheme that trains directly on the model's own autoregressive rollouts, with an adaptation of a contrastive diffusion RL objective to x0-prediction backbones.
Proposes a sensible variable-length prefix branching protocol that creates shared-context candidate groups for autoregressive video, enabling group-relative reward comparison.
Designs multi-view, clip-level perceptual rewards and group normalization, and supports them with object-centric and robot-centric masked evaluations.
Reports strong empirical results on DROID: consistent gains across metrics, ~98% paired wins, and an 80% blind human preference rate, with additional ablations in the appendix.
The paper is generally clear, provides implementation details, includes a derivation, and acknowledges key limitations such as compute overhead and reliance on visual fidelity rewards.
weaknesses: The main evaluation metrics (LPIPS, SSIM, PSNR) are also used as training rewards, so quantitative gains may partly reflect reward optimization rather than fully independent measures of world-model quality; the human study and masked evaluation mitigate but do not eliminate this concern.

Generalization evidence is limited: experiments use a single base model (Ctrl-World) and a single dataset (DROID), leaving unclear how well the approach transfers to other world-model backbones, datasets, or embodiments.

The closest contemporary method [36] is discussed but not empirically compared, despite sharing the core RL post-training idea; this weakens the claim of state-of-the-art relative to the most relevant recent work.

The theoretical claim that convergence guarantees carry over exactly rests on idealized assumptions such as unlimited data/model capacity, an exact reference posterior mean, and rewards interpreted as true optimality probabilities; it does not rigorously establish convergence for practical LoRA-based fine-tuning.
Computational cost is substantial (K=16 candidates, LoRA fine-tuning on 8 H200 GPUs for 3 days), and the paper does not quantify the trade-off between training overhead and rollout-quality gains.
The human preference study is relatively small (8 expert raters, moderate inter-rater agreement), which limits external validity and may not fully capture broader perceptual quality.
The main paper does not demonstrate downstream benefits such as improved policy learning or planning; the policy-evaluation correlation study is preliminary and relegated to the appendix.

Some design choices are not fully optimized or justified, e.g., best-of-2 filtering appears stronger than the chosen best-of-5 setting in ablations, with the final choice motivated mainly by stability/efficiency rather than best performance.

strengths: Targets a real and important failure mode in action-conditioned video world models: exposure bias and error compounding during long-horizon autoregressive rollouts.

Provides a plausible adaptation of contrastive diffusion RL/DiffusionNFT-style post-training to the x0-prediction EDM parameterization used by Ctrl-World, with a self-contained derivation in the appendix.
Introduces a practical variable-length prefix/branch rollout protocol that enables group-relative reward comparison for autoregressive video generation, where no fixed prompt exists.

Reports substantial empirical gains on DROID across multiple metrics and camera views, including object-centric and robot-centric masked evaluations, and supports these with a blind human preference study and policy-evaluation/policy-improvement experiments.

Includes generalization experiments beyond DROID (Bridge, RT-1) and a comparison to a Self-Forcing-style baseline, which strengthens the empirical case that the RL-style objective adds value beyond simply training on corrupted histories.
weaknesses: The 'RL' framing is somewhat overstated: the reward is a fixed perceptual similarity to ground-truth frames, and the update is essentially a reward-weighted supervised/contrastive regression on self-generated rollouts. It is not clear that standard RL or policy-gradient claims are warranted, nor that the method optimizes task success rather than visual similarity to recorded trajectories.

The theoretical claim that convergence guarantees 'carry over exactly' is not supported. Appendix A proves a property of the optimal predictor under infinite data/capacity and assumes the reward weight is a calibrated conditional probability P(o=1|x0,c). In practice r is a group-normalized rank score, so the stated guarantee does not directly apply to the implemented algorithm.

There is a serious ambiguity about data usage: the reward during training is computed against 'held-out ground-truth frames', while the paper also says the 'held-out validation split' is used for all quantitative evaluations. If the same validation split frames are used as reward targets during post-training, the main results are compromised by train/evaluation leakage; the paper must clearly separate reward-training data from evaluation data.

The main and appendix metrics are inconsistent: e.g., main Table 1 reports Ours external LPIPS 0.070 and PSNR 24.42, while appendix ablation defaults report external LPIPS ~0.116 and PSNR ~25.52. Such differences could be due to different rollout lengths or metric implementations, but the paper does not reconcile them, which undermines confidence in the ablation conclusions and comparability across tables.

Ablation evidence is often weak: many tables show differences within noise (e.g., KL regularization, old-policy EMA, learning-policy EMA, random vs. curriculum prefix sampling), and some design choices that perform better in the ablations (e.g., best-of-2) are not used in the final model. The claimed superiority of several design decisions is therefore not strongly supported.

Baseline comparisons are selective: WPE and IRASim numbers are taken from prior work, while Ctrl-World is both reproduced and cited with different numbers. Gains are sometimes reported against the weaker reproduced Ctrl-World† rather than the stronger Ctrl-World* baseline, which inflates relative improvements.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity and reproducibility: notation for H, L, F, and prefix length is inconsistent across the main text and appendix; algorithm pseudocode has malformed equations; the training data split for rewards is not specified; and key details such as branch length F and candidate subsampling are not fully integrated into the main method description.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: exposure bias and compounding errors in autoregressive robot world models.
The proposed variable-prefix branching protocol is simple and sensible for creating comparable candidate continuations from a shared autoregressive state.
Combines multiple perceptual metrics across camera views into a clip-level reward, which is a reasonable practical design for multi-view robot video generation.
Reports strong empirical gains over the reproduced Ctrl-World baseline on DROID, including improvements on both external and wrist cameras.
Includes object- and robot-centric masked evaluations, which help support the claim that gains are not merely background preservation.
Provides promising downstream evidence: improved world-model-based policy evaluation correlation and policy improvement over Ctrl-World in real-robot trials.
Adds a blind human preference study, which, despite limitations, strengthens the perceptual evaluation beyond automated metrics.
Demonstrates generalization beyond DROID to Bridge and RT-1, suggesting the post-training procedure is not entirely dataset-specific.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is substantially overclaimed. The paper repeatedly claims 'convergence guarantees carry over exactly,' but Appendix A only analyzes the unique minimizer under unlimited data, unlimited model capacity, and strong distributional assumptions. No convergence proof for gradient-based optimization is provided.

The claim that 'β→0 recovers standard supervised denoising against the reference' is mathematically incorrect. When β=0, both constructed branches collapse to the frozen reference prediction, and the loss becomes independent of the current model, so there is no supervised update to the current model.

The derivation treats the normalized reward r as the posterior probability of an optimality label, P(o=1|x0,c). In practice, r is obtained by group-wise z-scoring, clipping, and rescaling of perceptual metrics. It is not calibrated as such a probability, so the theorem does not directly apply to the method actually trained.

There is a serious ambiguity about train/validation leakage. The post-training reward requires ground-truth future frames, and the paper says evaluation uses Ctrl-World's held-out validation split. It is not clearly stated whether the reward computation uses training-split or validation-split ground truth. If validation frames are used for reward, the reported validation results are not held out.

The empirical evidence lacks rigor. No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported for the main metrics or ablations, despite many ablation differences being within noise (e.g., KL regularization, old-policy EMA, policy EMA, learning rate comparisons).

Several ablation results contradict the stated design choices. For example, in Table 5, fixed prefix size 3 and random 0-4 outperform the chosen random 0-9 on multiple metrics; in Table 4, the combined reward is not best on any individual metric despite being claimed as the necessary regularizer; in Table 6, best-of-2 outperforms the chosen best-of-5 on all reported metrics.

The comparison to WorldCompass [41] is inadequate. It is a concurrent, highly related work applying contrastive RL post-training to a world model with prefix rollouts, yet the paper does not report a direct quantitative comparison on DROID. The HPSv3 reward ablation is not apples-to-apples because HPSv3 expects text conditioning, and the paper acknowledges it cannot assess action-conditioned consistency.

The 'Self-Forcing style baseline' is misnamed and weak. It appears to be a self-conditioned supervised fine-tuning baseline that regresses ground-truth latents, not Self-Forcing, which typically involves distillation from a bidirectional teacher. This makes the comparison misleading and does not establish the advantage of the RL objective over proper alternatives.

The main text and appendix contain inconsistencies. KL regularization and old-policy EMA schedules appear in the appendix as part of 'Ours' but are not described in the main training objective. Notation for H, L, F, and P is confusing across sections and tables.

The SOTA claim is limited by the baseline set. The paper compares mainly to Ctrl-World, WPE, and IRASim, and does not include more recent action-conditioned world models or the concurrent WorldCompass. The reproduced Ctrl-World numbers also differ from the published ones without a clear explanation, weakening the state-of-the-art claim.

The human study has methodological weaknesses. It uses only 8 in-house experts, permits raters to choose which videos to rate, does not report how many were skipped, and does not fully analyze possible selection or expertise bias. The 80% preference rate is therefore less conclusive than presented.

The downstream policy-improvement experiment uses only 5 trials per block and lacks uncertainty estimates. The reported +19% gain over Ctrl-World is promising but not statistically supported as presented.

The reward weighting is questionable. LPIPS is negated but its typical scale (~0.1) is much smaller than SSIM (~0.8) and PSNR/32 (~0.7), so the reward may be dominated by SSIM and PSNR. The paper does not justify this balance beyond an informal scale-matching argument.

The paper does not adequately discuss computational overhead. The group-relative training with K=16 candidates per update is expensive, and while the limitation section acknowledges this, the practical trade-off against simpler self-conditioned fine-tuning or best-of-N alternatives is not quantified.

strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and underexplored problem: exposure bias and closed-loop degradation in action-conditioned video world models, with a clear formulation of the train/test mismatch.

Introduces a practical RL-style post-training scheme for autoregressive robot world models, adapting contrastive denoising from DiffusionNFT to the x0-prediction EDM parameterization and deriving the corresponding objective in the appendix.

The variable-length prefix branching protocol is a sensible contribution: it creates comparable candidate continuations from a shared corrupted history state, and the randomized horizon exposes training to multiple error regimes.
Multi-view perceptual rewards with group normalization and masked object/robot-centric evaluations help demonstrate that improvements are not merely background preservation.

Empirical evidence is broad: state-of-the-art visual metrics on DROID, large paired-comparison win rates, a blind human preference study, generalization to Bridge and RT-1, policy-evaluation correlation, and a policy-improvement experiment.
The paper is generally well written, includes implementation details, ablations, pseudocode, and a limitations section, which supports reproducibility and critical assessment.
weaknesses: Theoretical claims are somewhat overstated. The appendix proves an idealized optimal-predictor result under unlimited data/model capacity and assumes the reference model equals the posterior mean; this is not a full convergence or policy-improvement guarantee for the autoregressive, multi-step, LoRA-finetuned setting.

The reward computation relies on ground-truth future frames. If the same DROID validation split is used both for reward signal during post-training and for final evaluation, this would constitute test-target leakage and would inflate the reported gains; the paper should explicitly confirm that rewards are computed only from training trajectories or otherwise disjoint data.

Comparison to concurrent/related RL world-model post-training methods is incomplete. WorldCompass [41] is only compared via a reward swap rather than as a full method, so the contribution relative to the closest recent work is not fully isolated.

Some quantitative gains are modest on external cameras, and the wrist-camera table includes only Ctrl-World as a reproduced baseline; broader baseline coverage for all camera views would strengthen the claims.

The human preference study uses only 8 expert raters, and inter-rater agreement is moderate (kappa ~0.4), so the 80% preference result, while statistically significant, could be strengthened with a larger and more diverse rater pool.

The method optimizes perceptual metrics rather than physical or geometric consistency, which is acknowledged as a limitation, but it leaves open whether the improved rollouts are genuinely better for downstream control or primarily better on the reward metrics used for training.
Computational cost is non-trivial (8 H200 GPUs for 2 days, K=16 candidates per update), and the paper does not analyze the trade-off between post-training cost and downstream benefit in much depth.
